A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, theoretical argument, and benchmark construction. Text, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison; relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V2 reports original GNN training experiments on synthetic and SuiteSparse matrices, plus numerical comparisons of K-optimal and IC(0) preconditioners in Appendix A.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark experiments and additionally reports virtual-node and positional-encoding experiments in Appendices A–B.

M1.justification: V3 adds evaluated GNN adaptations using a node connected to every other node and triangular-position edge features valued −1/+1. These change information propagation and model inputs. The core K-optimal construction, encoder–processor–decoder design, and cosine-similarity objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic tridiagonal factorization problems and a collection drawn from 150 SuiteSparse symmetric positive definite matrices. The new virtual-node and positional-encoding experiments use these existing benchmark families; no additional domain or task is introduced.

E2.justification: The original six neural architectures and the K-optimal/IC(0) references remain. V3 additionally evaluates virtual-node variants and a positional-encoding MessagePassingMLP variant in Appendices A–B. FastGraphTransformer and GlobalGraphTransformer refer to the same cited comparator, so that renaming alone is not an addition.

E3.justification: Equation 8 changes the stated synthetic target from chol(A_i) to chol(A_i^m), matching the perturbed input; this establishes a reported protocol correction, not that experiments were rerun. The SuiteSparse global-transformer plot reduces the evaluated depth range from 1–7 to 1–3 blocks. Existing training budgets, batch sizes, and synthetic sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial controls addressing two central objections: whether virtual-node aggregation overcomes limited information propagation, and whether triangular-position features improve learning. Figures 5–6 test virtual nodes across architectures and both benchmarks; Figure 7 tests positional encodings with MessagePassingMLP. These analyses are absent from v2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The multiple plotted curves represent model depths rather than repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: V3 adds the virtual-node and positional-encoding results in Figures 5–7 and revises the global-transformer curves in both main benchmarks. The new controls retain substantial approximation gaps. Other main model curves largely match, and the relocated preconditioner pie chart retains 58.1%, 24.4%, 8.1%, and 9.3%. The revised results do not establish an overall same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Section 6.3 adds the formal observation that lower-triangular extraction does not commute with arbitrary permutations, expressed through an inequality for the learned mapping. Theorem 2.1, its proof, and the K-optimal derivation remain substantively unchanged; replacing X with G in the derivation is notation only.

C1.justification: The central contributions—nonlocality limitations, benchmark construction, and the need for suitable architectures—remain. The abstract revises its quantitative summary from cosine similarity below 0.6 in key cases to at most 0.7. The architecture-mismatch wording largely restates the earlier position.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands the interpretation and scope qualifications. It acknowledges that sufficiently deep message passing can implement Cholesky, explains depth plateaus and virtual-node bottlenecks, discusses order dependence and excluded coarsening/reordering strategies, and clarifies the offline role of K-optimal references. It also explicitly cautions against generalizing these findings to all neural scientific solvers.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies all-ones node inputs, the global transformer's attention/local-GATv2 mixture with alpha = 0.5, lower-triangular output extraction, and details of the added augmentations. The existing architecture widths, learning-rate schedule, hardware, and sample counts move from Appendix A.3 into Section 6.1 without substantive changes.

R1.justification: V3 adds connections to explicit message-passing linear algebra, virtual nodes, positional features, multigrid, equivariance, and matrix reordering, including Moore et al. (2025), Southern et al. (2024), and Häusner et al. (2024). These extend the retained research positioning. Bibliographic updates to works such as Wu and Luo are not new cited works.

P1.justification: The seven-section main outline and much of the original prose remain. V3 edits the abstract and terminology, expands selected explanatory passages and the discussion, integrates the old appendix's algorithm and implementation material into the main text, and reorganizes the appendices around the new analyses.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a different publication layout, typography, author arrangement, and recurring headers. It enlarges and redraws plots, standardizes learning-curve axes to 0.4–1.0, relocates and relabels the preconditioner pie chart, moves Algorithm 1 into the main text, and adds Figures 5–7.

improvement.justification: The new global-information and ordering controls, clearer depth and applicability qualifications, additional implementation details, and corrected Equation 8 make the negative findings easier to assess and reproduce. The narrower SuiteSparse global-transformer depth sweep modestly reduces existing evidence. Overall, these changes provide a limited net improvement while retaining the core theory and benchmark scope.
